title: Counting it loss (Philippians 3:1–11)
hook: everything Paul was proud of, he counts as loss compared with knowing Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Epaphroditus, two helpers named in a letter, and your line was hold such in honor.

A résumé, printed on the good paper. Born into the right family. The best teachers. A record nobody can fault. Then the owner takes a red pen and writes across the whole page: loss. Not shredding it. Not lying about it. Just marking it down, as if the numbers had been in the wrong column all along. That's close to what Paul does in the third chapter of Philippians. He lays out every credential he had, then moves the whole list to the other side of the ledger.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee." He kept the law of his people with great zeal, and says that by its measure of righteousness he was blameless. He isn't mocking any of it. These are real goods: an honored family, a faithful upbringing, a serious life. "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." It's bookkeeping language: gain and loss. Then he goes further: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." All things. And he uses a rough word for them, one that means refuse, the scraps you throw out. Older English Bibles put it bluntly as dung. Why so strong? Because what he wants now is not a record but a person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings." Know, here, is not knowing about. It's the way you know a friend. Christians read this passage in different ways. Some hear a conversion from one way of standing before God to another. Others stress that Paul never stops being a Jew, and that what he counts as loss is his own standing, his pride, not the Torah or his people. Both readings see the turn: the things that once defined him no longer get to.
screen: then, large: `I COUNT ALL THINGS BUT LOSS.`

segments.voice: Name something you're proud of that quietly runs your life: a title, a grade, being the one who's always right, or always busy, or always fine. It may be a real good, as Paul's were, so don't throw it away; just picture writing it on a card and moving it out of the center, and notice what's left in the middle. If you pray, you can hand it to God and leave the card there.
Pharisee. Paul's own credential before his bookkeeping turn: a label he moved, with everything else he had, into the loss column, next to knowing Christ.
Your line: all else is loss. A record, traded for a person. That's day six hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians read Philippians 3 when thinking about pride and identity, and some churches use verses 7 to 11 in Lent as a reflection on what to set aside.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you have the family, the training and a spotless record. what do you do with it?
options: lead with it, so people trust you.
count it all as loss compared with knowing Christ.
fork.reveal: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." he doesn't hide the list. he re-files it.

original.note: Greek: loss, damage, a business write-off. Paul uses it in verses 7 and 8.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul saying his past was bad.
what it means: his real goods, family, law, zeal, re-counted as loss beside knowing Christ.
what a scholar hears: gain and loss are ledger words; some scholars today read the loss as Paul's own standing and pride, not a rejection of his people or the Torah.

chat.says: Why did Paul call his whole impressive background loss? Was he ashamed of it?
options: No, they were real goods, but next to knowing Christ he no longer let them define him.
Yes, he came to think his family and upbringing were shameful and wrong.
No, he meant he'd lost everything in prison and was simply sad about it.
chat.meaning: Paul isn't mocking his credentials; he counts them loss "for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ": a person, not a record.

Pharisee.meaning: a member of a Jewish group devoted to keeping the law

tribe of Benjamin.meaning: one of Israel's twelve tribes, Paul's own

Torah.meaning: the law of Moses, the first books of the Hebrew Bible

Philippians.meaning: Paul's letter to the church at Philippi

notes: Greek σκύβαλα (3:8): refuse, scraps, sometimes dung; the KJV has 'dung'. Confirm the gloss.
ζημία appears in 3:7 and 3:8 (with the related verb ἐζημιώθην in 3:8). Confirm.

The two readings (conversion of standing; the 'new perspective' stress that Paul remains a Jew and counts his own standing as loss) are given without ranking. Confirm fairness to Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox readers and to Jewish listeners.
